technologies.name: Drum
technologies.description:
Structure of the magnetographic drum
![Drum animation](/assets/collections/magnetographie/anim_tambour.gif)
The original drum has a diameter of 100 mm (≈4 inches). Its body is hollow. Initially built up from a stack of Fe-Si washers (a lamination intended to minimise eddy currents), it was very soon replaced by an aluminium tube. Its surface carries a layer of Fe-Ni (a magnetically soft material, providing an efficient closure path for the write fluxes), then a Co-Ni-P layer (a magnetically hard material, used to "store" the written dots). These two layers, a few tens of microns thick, are obtained by electrodeposition. A third, very thin Mo-C layer, applied by sputtering, provides protection against wear. Drum lifetime reaches 20 to 30 million pages.
A drum 6 inches in diameter was introduced in the third-generation products. At the same time, the increase in print speeds made it necessary to cool the drum by circulating water inside its hollow body.

technologies.name: Writing
technologies.description:
Recording the latent magnetic image

Click on the module extracted from the write bar to learn more about its structure…

The latent magnetic image is written onto the drum by a set of write modules (10 of them in the first machines) which, positioned along a generatrix of the drum, record microlines of dots (up to 3,336 dots per microline in the first machines, with a density of 240 dpi).
Energising a write pole creates a magnetic field perpendicular to the drum surface, which locally magnetises the Co-Ni-P layer. Once the write command is switched off and the magnetic field has relaxed, the area concerned remains magnetised.
![Photo of the modules](/assets/collections/magnetographie/modules.webp)
With the third-generation machines, a 480 dpi high-definition module was introduced in 1997. Unlike the original module, essentially based on micromechanical processes, the new module makes extensive use of silicon microelectronic processes. The write bar is then made up of 18 modules, aligned in two alternating rows, providing a microline of 8,640 dots.
![Bar](/assets/collections/magnetographie/barre.gif)
A very-high-definition 600 dpi version, extrapolated from the same technologies, equips the fourth-generation machines (2000s onward).

technologies.name: Module
technologies.description:
Module of parallel magnetographic heads

Click at the centre of the diagram to learn more about how the head works, as well as the new-generation 480 and 600 dpi heads. 

The G1 (generation 1) module has 336 discrete heads, arranged in 6 groups (sub-modules), the heads of each group being addressable within a diode matrix of 7 sequential selection lines and 8 data lines.

![Photo](/assets/collections/magnetographie/barre.gif)

The overmoulding of the module incorporates, in a single block, the 336 heads, the 336 diodes, the connections and the protective pads located on either side of the line of write poles.

The write bar carries 10 modules side by side, giving a total of 3,336 heads at a pitch of 240 per inch.

technologies.name: Head
technologies.description:
Writing the dots of the latent magnetic image

In the first commercial products (240 dpi), the individual head consists of a high-magnetic-permeability Fe-Ni track (50 µm thick), with a narrow write pole, a greatly elongated return pole and a winding (90 turns).
Energising the winding (≈ 100 mA) creates a magnetic flux channelled by the track which, leaving the write pole, passes vertically through the drum's Co-Ni-P layer, then through the Fe-Ni underlayer, before closing back through the return pole.
By the law of conservation of magnetic flux, the induction directly beneath the write pole is far higher than that prevailing under the return pole.
After the current is switched off and the magnetic materials have relaxed, the recorded dot retains a magnetisation, while that at the return pole is practically negligible.

High-Definition Heads

The operating principle of the write head in the 480 dpi HD module (found on the third-generation machines) is not fundamentally different: recording on the drum remains of the perpendicular type, produced by a vertical write pole. The flat coil offers better efficiency, and the flux return poles are advantageously replaced by a return plane common to all the poles of a given module.

![480 dpi head](/assets/collections/magnetographie/Tete_480_dpi.png)

The essential difference lies in the manufacturing techniques: discrete micromechanical processes are replaced by the batch processes of silicon microelectronics. The module comprises a silicon chip with 480 write poles and 480 co-integrated diodes. A flat cable connects the chip to its connector.

Development of these new write heads began in 1991, and the 480 dpi definition was raised to 600 dpi in 2000.
To learn more, you can consult the presentation by B. Cherbuy (who initiated and oversaw this project): IS&T Congress, New Orleans, October 1994

technologies.name: Inking
technologies.description:
Developing the latent image with toner

The ink used is of the dry powder type (usually called "toner"). The toner particles, magnetised beforehand, are applied to the drum surface by a magnetic conveyor consisting of a continuously rotating cylinder that "lifts" the ink into contact with the image. The magnetic "dots" making up the latent image retain the ink particles, while the non-imaged areas remain almost untouched.
When stationary or at very low speed, however, the toner tends to produce background noise by adhering to the drum even where there is no image. This background noise decreases as speed increases, owing to the ever more energetic collisions between free particles and captive particles in the inking zone.
![Inked dot](/assets/collections/magnetographie/Dot_encre.png)
The dots, for their part, tend to become covered with too much ink. An adjustable magnetic touch-up, supplemented by air-blade suction, removes the excess toner.
Historically, the first machines used an inking "bed", almost static but with a high particle density, created by a barrier blade placed across the flow of particles. The second-generation machines favoured inking by a fluidised wave generated by a springboard blade.

technologies.name: Transfer
technologies.description:
Electrostatic transfer of the toner onto the paper
Principle of transfer
In the first machines, transferring the inked image onto the paper relied solely on the pressure exerted by a roller located behind the paper. This purely mechanical solution offered the advantage of perfect synchronism between the drum and the paper web, but suffered from a relatively low transfer rate.
Electrostatic assistance very soon proved necessary. Polarising the metal core of the transfer roller, with the drum connected to earth, generates an electric field in the transfer zone. The toner particles, of resistive type and pre-charged upstream by a DC corotron, interact with this electric field, which helps detach them from the drum.
Finally, a second corotron, this time an AC one, dissipates the electrostatic charges of the paper in the post-transfer zone.

technologies.name: Fusing
technologies.description:
Fusing the heat-fusible toner onto the paper

The final fixing of the image, once inked and transferred onto the paper, consists of melting the heat-fusible toner so that it penetrates the paper fibres and anchors itself firmly there as it cools.
Physically, the resin of the particles goes through the following phases:

- solid state (room temperature), hard particles of irregular shape
- viscoelastic state (temperature > glass transition temperature Tg), tendency to spheroidise
- viscous fluid state (temperature > melting temperature Tf), coalescence of the particles into a single mass
- the fluid mass flows and wets the irregularities of the paper
- cooling (room temperature)

The first machines use fusing by a continuous radiant oven: the paper web passes under an assembly of halogen lamps and a reflector. The paper itself is pre-heated by contact with a heated platen. The third-generation machines saw the introduction of flash fusing, which has the advantage of heating only the toner and hardly the paper at all.

technologies.name: Cleaning
technologies.description:
Cleaning off the untransferred toner residues

Cleaning of the drum relies essentially on a metal scraper blade. The toner residues thus detached are removed by suction.
A felt pad located behind the blade completes the cleaning operation.

technologies.name: Erasing
technologies.description:
Resetting by an AC magnetic erase head

Once the toner has been transferred and the drum cleaned, the magnetic image still has to be erased so that the next print cycle can begin.
This operation is classically performed with a magnetic head of the so-called "leakage" type. The magnetic field created by an alternating current produces, in space, an alternating field of decreasing amplitude. The dots of the magnetic image, moving away from the erase head as the drum rotates, are exposed to this field. Their magnetic state describes minor hysteresis loops that rapidly tend towards zero.
